idea: A dependency graph separates what can run concurrently from what must wait. The critical path bounds completion time even with unlimited workers.
steps: Topologically order tasks and reject cycles.
Compute earliest/latest times to identify zero-slack critical tasks.
List-schedule ready tasks on the worker pool; longest ready task wins.
example: Two independent tasks lasting 4 and 3 finish in 4 with two workers, but 7 with one.
concepts: Every predecessor appears before its dependent.
Latest start minus earliest start under unlimited resources.
Limited-worker list scheduling is deterministic but not globally optimal.
question: Does zero slack mean a worker is always busy?
answer: No. Slack is computed from dependencies alone. Actual resource contention can create additional waiting.
challenge: Reduce workers from two to one and compare the critical bound with the actual schedule.
cost: Topology/critical passes O(V+E), with heap ordering overhead; scheduling here scans pending tasks.
